**Cross-Layer Probabilistic Compatibility Propagation with Self-Calibrating Constraints for Autonomous AI Agent Stack Assembly**

# Problem Statement

AI agent deployments are built from multiple interdependent software layers: foundation models, prompt templates, orchestration frameworks, tool connectors, and runtime environments. Upgrading any single layer can break the others through cross-layer interactions that nobody has formally quantified. This is not like traditional package dependencies where version mismatches produce hard failures. AI stack incompatibilities show up as continuous performance degradation. A tokenizer change will not crash a prompt template, but it will silently inflate its token consumption, and accuracy drops by a measurable amount that only surfaces after expensive benchmark runs. Engineers discover these probabilistic incompatibilities through trial and error.

With weekly ecosystem releases and organizations running dozens of agents, the compatibility assessment burden compounds fast. No existing system models cross-layer compatibility as a probabilistic constraint problem. None reason about continuous degradation gradients across all stack layers at once. And none refine their own compatibility predictions from observed outcomes.

# Description of Invention

## Novel Step

We introduce a probabilistic cross-layer compatibility propagation mechanism that models every AI agent stack component as a node in a compatibility graph. Edges encode machine-readable interface contracts that express compatibility as continuous confidence scores rather than Boolean pass/fail verdicts. When a new component is discovered from external registries, the system performs probabilistic constraint propagation across this graph, computing expected compatibility scores and confidence intervals for each candidate stack combination. The propagation reasons about transitive degradation gradients: a model's tokenizer vocabulary change may inflate a prompt template's effective token consumption by an estimated 35% to 45%, which narrows the context budget available for tool call results in the orchestration layer, which we predict reduces end-to-end task accuracy by 8% to 12% with 90% confidence. Combinations whose predicted compatibility falls below configurable thresholds get pruned before any evaluation infrastructure is provisioned.

Critically, we include a closed-loop calibration mechanism. After each evaluation cycle, observed benchmark results are compared against the constraint solver's predictions, and the system automatically adjusts predicate thresholds, confidence interval widths, and degradation coefficients to improve future prediction accuracy. This self-calibrating constraint model has no analog in traditional dependency resolution systems (apt, npm, Helm, Kubernetes OLM), which resolve hard version constraints and cannot express or learn from continuous compatibility gradients. Each promoted stack carries a standardized Stack Compatibility Manifest embedded in deployment metadata and queryable through a compatibility negotiation API, producing externally detectable artifacts that distinguish this system from ad hoc integration approaches.

## How It Works

We model the AI agent software stack as a directed compatibility graph. Each node represents a versioned component: a specific model release, a prompt template revision, an orchestration framework version, a tool connector build, or a runtime configuration. Edges between nodes carry probabilistic interface contracts, which are machine-readable declarations of what each component provides to and requires from adjacent layers. These are expressed as continuous compatibility functions rather than Boolean predicates.

Every component in the system carries an interface contract expressed in a standardized metadata schema with both hard constraints and soft compatibility parameters. For a foundation model, the contract declares the tokenizer type, vocabulary size, maximum context window in tokens, supported input and output formats (chat completion, raw completion, function calling), resource requirements (GPU memory, system memory, compute features such as specific CUDA versions or attention implementations), and explicit incompatibilities as hard constraints. It also declares soft parameters: measured token density ratios for common text types (English prose, code, structured JSON), empirical latency profiles under different quantization levels, and historical accuracy baselines on reference tasks.

For a prompt template, the contract declares hard constraints such as required model capabilities (tool calling support, system prompt handling) and input/output variable schemas. Soft parameters include the token budget expressed as a distribution across tokenizer families. A template might consume 1800 to 2200 tokens with SentencePiece tokenizers and 1600 to 1900 with BPE, depending on content. It also includes sensitivity coefficients that quantify how much accuracy degrades per percentage of context budget consumed, and a compatibility history recording observed performance with specific model versions. For an orchestration framework, the contract declares supported chain patterns, maximum tool call depth, memory backend requirements, and minimum available context token thresholds as hard constraints. Soft parameters capture throughput degradation curves as context use approaches limits. For a runtime environment, the contract declares available compute features, memory limits, supported container images, and scaling characteristics, with soft parameters expressing performance variability under different load levels.

The Component Discovery Service periodically polls external registries, including model hubs, package repositories, and internal artifact stores, and normalizes each discovered component into this contract schema. Staleness detection runs on a configurable cadence so that deprecated or withdrawn components are flagged and excluded from future candidate generation. When a new component is ingested, the system inserts the corresponding node into the compatibility graph and evaluates probabilistic constraint functions on every edge connecting the new node to existing nodes in adjacent layers.

A constraint function differs fundamentally from the Boolean predicates used in traditional dependency resolution. Rather than returning true or false, each constraint function returns a compatibility score between 0.0 and 1.0 along with a confidence interval reflecting the system's certainty in that estimate. For example, a tokenizer compatibility function between a model and a prompt template does not merely check whether tokenizer types match. Instead, it computes the expected token count variance when the template is tokenized by the model's tokenizer, derives a predicted accuracy impact from the template's sensitivity coefficients, and produces a compatibility score such as 0.72 with a confidence interval of plus or minus 0.08 at 90% confidence. That 0.72 means the combination is expected to retain 72% of baseline accuracy for that cross-layer interaction. It is not a probability of success. This continuous representation captures the reality that AI stack incompatibilities are not binary: a tokenizer mismatch does not crash the system but degrades performance by a quantifiable amount that may or may not be acceptable depending on organizational policy.

When a new component is added to the graph, the system performs forward probabilistic constraint propagation through all downstream layers. The algorithm works in three stages. First, it evaluates all direct constraint functions between the new component and every existing component in the adjacent layer, computing pairwise compatibility scores with confidence intervals. Second, for each pairing that exceeds the minimum score threshold, it propagates forward to the next layer: given a particular model paired with a particular prompt template, their combined characteristics (effective available context after prompt consumption, accumulated resource footprint, predicted accuracy retention) feed into constraint functions against each candidate orchestration framework. Compatibility scores compose multiplicatively across layers, so a 0.85 model-to-prompt score combined with a 0.90 prompt-to-orchestrator score yields a cumulative cross-layer score of approximately 0.77. Third, propagation continues through tool connectors and runtime layers, accumulating both resource requirements and compounding compatibility scores. The confidence intervals widen as propagation deepens, reflecting increasing uncertainty in multi-hop predictions.

This probabilistic propagation is where the system's value becomes concrete and where it diverges most sharply from traditional dependency resolution. Consider a tokenizer vocabulary expansion in a new model release. A traditional Boolean constraint system would either pass or fail based on a type match check. Our system instead computes that the vocabulary expansion will increase the prompt template's token consumption by an estimated 38% (confidence interval: 33% to 43%), which reduces the effective context available for the orchestration layer's tool call results from 12,000 tokens to approximately 7,400 tokens. The orchestration layer's throughput degradation curve indicates that at 7,400 available tokens, tool call truncation will occur in roughly 15% of invocations. Composing these effects, we predict a cumulative accuracy retention of 0.71 with a confidence interval of 0.65 to 0.77 for the full stack. If organizational policy requires a minimum cumulative score of 0.80, this combination is pruned without provisioning any infrastructure, but it is preserved as a near-miss candidate that could become viable if the prompt template is revised to reduce its token footprint. A Boolean solver cannot express this kind of graduated analysis. It cannot distinguish between a combination that misses the threshold by 0.01 and one that scores 0.15.

The self-calibrating feedback loop is the mechanism that makes the constraint model improve over time, and it has no counterpart in traditional dependency resolution systems. After each evaluation cycle, the Calibration Engine compares the constraint solver's predicted compatibility scores against observed benchmark results. For every evaluated stack, the engine computes a prediction residual: the difference between the predicted cumulative compatibility score and the normalized actual performance measured during benchmarking. These residuals are aggregated by constraint function, by component pair type, and by layer transition, revealing systematic biases in the constraint model.

If the tokenizer compatibility function consistently overestimates compatibility for SentencePiece-to-BPE transitions by 0.12, the calibration engine adjusts the function's degradation coefficients downward and widens the confidence intervals for that transition type until prediction accuracy improves. If the orchestrator context budget function consistently underestimates throughput impact at low available token counts, the engine reshapes the throughput degradation curve to better match observed behavior. Updates are applied using an exponentially weighted moving average over recent evaluation cycles, with a configurable learning rate that balances responsiveness to new data against stability. Updates are bounded by configurable maximum adjustment limits per cycle to prevent a single anomalous benchmark result from destabilizing the constraint model. The calibration engine also tracks overall prediction accuracy as a meta-metric. If prediction accuracy degrades, the engine flags the degradation for operator review and can optionally pause automatic updates.

What this self-calibrating mechanism creates is a compound advantage over systems that rely on statically defined constraints. As the system processes more evaluation cycles, its compatibility predictions become more precise, which improves pruning accuracy, which reduces wasted evaluation resources, which lets more evaluation budget go toward genuinely promising candidates, which generates more calibration data. The result is a system that becomes more efficient and more accurate with use. Static dependency resolution cannot achieve this property because its constraints are authored by humans and only change when humans update them.

The result of probabilistic constraint propagation is a ranked compatibility graph where each valid connected subgraph carries a cumulative compatibility score and confidence interval. The Stack Assembler generates candidate stack manifests only from subgraphs whose cumulative scores exceed the organization's minimum threshold, ranked by predicted performance. Rather than evaluating every possible permutation, the assembler uses a guided search strategy informed by organizational policy hints (such as preferences for open-weight models, license exclusions, or cost ceilings), historical performance data from previous evaluation cycles, and the calibration engine's confidence assessments. Candidates with narrow confidence intervals and high predicted scores are prioritized because they represent the most reliable predictions. This further narrows the search space so that only the most promising valid combinations proceed to evaluation. Each candidate stack is expressed as an immutable manifest that pins every component version, configuration parameter, dependency, and predicted compatibility score, making it fully reproducible.

Candidate stacks that survive constraint propagation are submitted to an Evaluation Orchestrator that provisions isolated execution environments and runs them against the organization's benchmark suite. The benchmark suite is a versioned artifact containing representative tasks, golden answer datasets, latency budgets, and cost accounting rules. The orchestrator collects metrics across multiple objectives: task accuracy, end-to-end latency, token consumption, infrastructure cost, and any custom signals the organization defines such as compliance audit pass rates or fairness scores. All evaluation results are stored in an append-only Performance Ledger that preserves the complete history of every evaluation alongside the benchmark version used, making sure that comparisons remain valid even as benchmarks evolve. The ledger also stores the constraint solver's predicted compatibility scores for each evaluated candidate, enabling the calibration engine to compute prediction residuals.

A Policy Engine consumes the Performance Ledger and makes promotion decisions based on declarative rules authored by operators. Operators express criteria such as "promote a candidate only if it improves accuracy by at least two percent without increasing p99 latency beyond 300 milliseconds, and only if the constraint solver's confidence interval width for the candidate was below 0.15." The policy engine supports multi-objective Pareto analysis, surfacing trade-offs between competing metrics explicitly rather than collapsing them into a single score. When a candidate satisfies all promotion criteria, the Policy Engine initiates a staged rollout through a Deployment Controller that shifts traffic gradually, monitors live signals, and automatically rolls back if regression thresholds are breached. The deployment controller integrates with the organization's existing service mesh or gateway infrastructure so that the optimization loop operates within established operational boundaries.

Each promoted stack carries a Stack Compatibility Manifest embedded in its deployment metadata. This manifest is a machine-readable document listing every component version in the stack, the interface contract version for each component, the probabilistic constraint functions that were evaluated with their predicted scores and confidence intervals, the calibration engine's current accuracy metrics for each constraint function, and a cryptographic provenance signature linking back to the evaluation evidence and the discovery events that introduced each component. The manifest appears in deployment annotations (such as Kubernetes pod annotations or labels), in registry metadata attached to promoted stack bundles, and in responses from the system's compatibility negotiation API endpoint. This endpoint accepts a set of proposed component versions and returns a probabilistic compatibility assessment: a predicted cumulative score with confidence interval, any constraint violations or degradation warnings, and resolution suggestions with their predicted score improvements. External tools and registries can query this endpoint to make informed compatibility decisions. The presence of these manifests in deployment metadata and the compatibility negotiation API protocol constitute externally observable fingerprints of the system's operation, distinguishable from manual stack assembly by their structured format, probabilistic constraint records, calibration metadata, and provenance signatures.

Throughout the lifecycle, a Provenance Tracker records every decision in a cryptographically signed, append-only ledger: why a candidate was assembled, which constraint functions evaluated its compatibility and at what predicted scores, which benchmark version evaluated it, what calibration adjustments were applied afterward, what policy rule promoted it, and what deployment strategy was used. This provenance chain gives operators a full audit trail from any production stack configuration back to the raw discovery event that introduced its components and the calibration history that informed the constraint model's predictions. Because every prior stack manifest and its evaluation data are preserved, the system can revert to any previously validated configuration within seconds rather than requiring a manual rebuild.

To make the value proposition concrete: consider an organization running 50 agents across 12 distinct stack configurations. When a new model version or framework update ships, engineers have to manually assess compatibility with each existing configuration. Without formalized interface contracts, each assessment requires reading changelogs, checking API compatibility, testing tokenizer behavior, and running integration tests. That process typically eats several hours per configuration. With 12 configurations and weekly ecosystem releases, the organization faces over 100 hours per month of compatibility assessment work, and roughly one in three migration attempts fails due to cross-layer conflicts that surface only during integration testing. Our probabilistic constraint propagation system reduces compatibility assessment to seconds per candidate and eliminates wasted evaluation cycles on combinations predicted to fall below performance thresholds. This recovers those engineering hours while preventing production incidents from incompatible stack deployments. As the calibration engine refines its predictions over successive evaluation cycles, pruning accuracy improves: early cycles might achieve 70% prediction accuracy, but after several months of operation the system typically reaches above 90%. That means nearly all pruned combinations would have genuinely failed evaluation and nearly all passed combinations genuinely succeed.

# --- Probabilistic Constraint Function Definitions ---
# These functions compute continuous compatibility scores
# with confidence intervals, not Boolean pass/fail verdicts.

constraint_functions:
  - name: tokenizer-compatibility
    source_layer: model
    target_layer: prompt_template
    type: probabilistic
    function: |
      IF target.token_budget_distribution[source.tokenizer.type] IS NULL:
        # No empirical data for this tokenizer type
        score = 0.50  # uncertain default
        confidence_interval = 0.25  # wide interval reflects ignorance
      ELSE:
        expected_tokens = target.token_budget_distribution[source.tokenizer.type].mean
        token_variance = target.token_budget_distribution[source.tokenizer.type].std_dev
        context_utilization = expected_tokens / source.context_window_tokens
        # Score decreases as prompt consumes more context
        score = max(0, 1.0 - (context_utilization * 2.0))
        # Confidence narrows with more empirical measurements
        n_measurements = len(target.token_budget_distribution[source.tokenizer.type].measured_on)
        confidence_interval = token_variance / (expected_tokens * sqrt(n_measurements))
      RETURN {score, confidence_interval, confidence_level: 0.90}
    calibration:
      current_bias: -0.03  # solver slightly overestimates; applied as correction
      last_calibrated: "2026-07-10T08:00:00Z"
      prediction_accuracy_last_30_days: 0.87

  - name: context-budget-impact
    source_layers: [model, prompt_template]
    target_layer: orchestration
    type: probabilistic
    function: |
      expected_prompt_tokens = prompt_template.token_budget_distribution[model.tokenizer.type].mean
      remaining_context = model.context_window_tokens - expected_prompt_tokens
      IF remaining_context < target.min_available_context_tokens:
        score = 0.0  # hard constraint: below absolute minimum
        confidence_interval = 0.0
      ELSE:
        # Interpolate on the throughput degradation curve
        truncation_rate = interpolate(target.throughput_degradation_curve, remaining_context)
        accuracy_impact = interpolate_accuracy(target.throughput_degradation_curve, remaining_context)
        score = 1.0 - accuracy_impact
        # Confidence depends on prompt token variance and curve granularity
        token_std = prompt_template.token_budget_distribution[model.tokenizer.type].std_dev
        context_range = [remaining_context - token_std, remaining_context + token_std]
        score_range = [
          1.0 - interpolate_accuracy(target.throughput_degradation_curve, context_range[0]),
          1.0 - interpolate_accuracy(target.throughput_degradation_curve, context_range[1])
        ]
        confidence_interval = abs(score_range[1] - score_range[0]) / 2
      RETURN {score, confidence_interval, confidence_level: 0.90}
    calibration:
      current_bias: +0.05  # solver underestimates; orchestrator handles truncation better than predicted
      last_calibrated: "2026-07-12T12:00:00Z"
      prediction_accuracy_last_30_days: 0.82

  - name: model-capabilities-match
    source_layer: model
    target_layer: prompt_template
    type: hard  # this remains Boolean; capabilities either exist or do not
    expression: |
      target.required_model_capabilities IS SUBSET OF source.capabilities
    failure_message: >
      Template requires capabilities not supported by model

  - name: runtime-resource-satisfaction
    source_layer: model
    target_layer: runtime
    type: hard  # resource requirements are binary
    expression: |
      source.resource_requirements.gpu_memory_gb <= target.gpu_memory_gb
      AND source.resource_requirements.required_features
        IS SUBSET OF target.available_features
    failure_message: >
      Model requires {source.resource_requirements.gpu_memory_gb}GB GPU
      but runtime provides {target.gpu_memory_gb}GB

# Problem Statement

AI agent deployments comprise multiple interdependent software layers: foundation models, prompt templates, orchestration frameworks, tool connectors, and runtime environments. Upgrading any single layer can degrade others through cross-layer interactions that are nowhere formally quantified. Unlike package dependencies where version mismatches produce hard failures, AI stack incompatibilities manifest as continuous performance degradation: a tokenizer change does not crash a prompt template but silently inflates its token consumption, reducing accuracy by a measurable amount that only surfaces after expensive benchmark runs. With weekly ecosystem releases and organizations running dozens of agents, the compatibility assessment burden compounds rapidly. # Description of Invention

## Novel Step

The system introduces a probabilistic cross-layer compatibility propagation mechanism that models every AI agent stack component as a node in a compatibility graph, with edges encoding machine-readable interface contracts that express compatibility as continuous confidence scores rather than Boolean pass/fail verdicts. When a new component is discovered from external registries, the system performs probabilistic constraint propagation across this graph, computing expected compatibility scores and confidence intervals for each candidate stack combination. This propagation reasons about transitive degradation gradients: a model's tokenizer vocabulary change may inflate a prompt template's effective token consumption by an estimated 35% to 45%, which narrows the context budget available for tool call results in the orchestration layer, which is predicted to reduce end-to-end task accuracy by 8% to 12% with 90% confidence. Combinations whose predicted compatibility falls below configurable thresholds are pruned before any evaluation infrastructure is provisioned. Critically, the system includes a closed-loop calibration mechanism: after each evaluation cycle, observed benchmark results are compared against the constraint solver's predictions, and the system automatically adjusts predicate thresholds, confidence interval widths, and degradation coefficients to improve future prediction accuracy. This self-calibrating constraint model has no analog in traditional dependency resolution systems (apt, npm, Helm, Kubernetes OLM), which resolve hard version constraints and cannot express or learn from continuous compatibility gradients. Each promoted stack carries a standardized Stack Compatibility Manifest embedded in deployment metadata and queryable through a compatibility negotiation API, producing externally detectable artifacts that distinguish this system from ad hoc integration approaches.

## How It Works

The system models the AI agent software stack as a directed compatibility graph. Each node represents a versioned component: a specific model release, a prompt template revision, an orchestration framework version, a tool connector build, or a runtime configuration. Edges between nodes carry probabilistic interface contracts, which are machine-readable declarations of what each component provides to and requires from adjacent layers, expressed as continuous compatibility functions rather than Boolean predicates.

Every component in the system carries an interface contract expressed in a standardized metadata schema with both hard constraints and soft compatibility parameters. For a foundation model, the contract declares the tokenizer type, vocabulary size, maximum context window in tokens, supported input and output formats (chat completion, raw completion, function calling), resource requirements (GPU memory, system memory, compute features such as specific CUDA versions or attention implementations), and explicit incompatibilities as hard constraints. It also declares soft parameters: measured token density ratios for common text types (English prose, code, structured JSON), empirical latency profiles under different quantization levels, and historical accuracy baselines on reference tasks. For a prompt template, the contract declares hard constraints such as required model capabilities (tool calling support, system prompt handling) and input/output variable schemas. Its soft parameters include the token budget expressed as a distribution across tokenizer families (a template might consume 1800 to 2200 tokens with SentencePiece tokenizers and 1600 to 1900 with BPE, depending on content), sensitivity coefficients that quantify how much accuracy degrades per percentage of context budget consumed, and a compatibility history recording observed performance with specific model versions. For an orchestration framework, the contract declares supported chain patterns, maximum tool call depth, memory backend requirements, and minimum available context token thresholds as hard constraints, with soft parameters capturing throughput degradation curves as context utilization approaches limits. For a runtime environment, the contract declares available compute features, memory limits, supported container images, and scaling characteristics, with soft parameters expressing performance variability under different utilization levels.

The Component Discovery Service periodically polls external registries, including model hubs, package repositories, and internal artifact stores, and normalizes each discovered component into this contract schema. Staleness detection runs on a configurable cadence so that deprecated or withdrawn components are flagged and excluded from future candidate generation. When a new component is ingested, the system inserts the corresponding node into the compatibility graph and evaluates probabilistic constraint functions on every edge connecting the new node to existing nodes in adjacent layers.

A constraint function differs fundamentally from the Boolean predicates used in traditional dependency resolution. Rather than returning true or false, each constraint function returns a compatibility score between 0.0 and 1.0 along with a confidence interval reflecting the system's certainty in that estimate. For example, a tokenizer compatibility function between a model and a prompt template does not merely check whether tokenizer types match. Instead, it computes the expected token count variance when the template is tokenized by the model's tokenizer, derives a predicted accuracy impact from the template's sensitivity coefficients, and produces a compatibility score such as 0.72 with a confidence interval of plus or minus 0.08 at 90% confidence. A score of 0.72 indicates the combination is expected to retain 72% of baseline accuracy for that cross-layer interaction, not that there is a 72% chance of success. This continuous representation captures the reality that AI stack incompatibilities are not binary: a tokenizer mismatch does not crash the system but degrades performance by a quantifiable amount that may or may not be acceptable depending on organizational policy.

When a new component is added to the graph, the system performs forward probabilistic constraint propagation through all downstream layers. The algorithm operates in three stages. First, it evaluates all direct constraint functions between the new component and every existing component in the adjacent layer, computing pairwise compatibility scores with confidence intervals. Second, for each pairing that exceeds the minimum score threshold, it propagates forward to the next layer: given a particular model paired with a particular prompt template, their combined characteristics (effective available context after prompt consumption, accumulated resource footprint, predicted accuracy retention) feed into constraint functions against each candidate orchestration framework. The compatibility scores compose multiplicatively across layers, so a 0.85 model-to-prompt score combined with a 0.90 prompt-to-orchestrator score yields a cumulative cross-layer score of approximately 0.77. Third, propagation continues through tool connectors and runtime layers, accumulating both resource requirements and compounding compatibility scores. The confidence intervals widen as propagation deepens, reflecting increasing uncertainty in multi-hop predictions.

This probabilistic propagation is where the system's value becomes concrete and where it diverges most sharply from traditional dependency resolution. Consider a tokenizer vocabulary expansion in a new model release. A traditional Boolean constraint system would either pass or fail based on a type match check. This system instead computes that the vocabulary expansion will increase the prompt template's token consumption by an estimated 38% (confidence interval: 33% to 43%), which reduces the effective context available for the orchestration layer's tool call results from 12,000 tokens to approximately 7,400 tokens. The orchestration layer's throughput degradation curve indicates that at 7,400 available tokens, tool call truncation will occur in approximately 15% of invocations. Composing these effects, the system predicts a cumulative accuracy retention of 0.71 with a confidence interval of 0.65 to 0.77 for the full stack. If organizational policy requires a minimum cumulative score of 0.80, this combination is pruned without provisioning any infrastructure, but it is preserved as a near-miss candidate that could become viable if the prompt template is revised to reduce its token footprint. A Boolean solver cannot express this graduated analysis and cannot distinguish between a combination that misses the threshold by 0.01 and one that scores 0.15.

The self-calibrating feedback loop is the mechanism that makes the constraint model improve over time and that has no counterpart in traditional dependency resolution systems. After each evaluation cycle, the Calibration Engine compares the constraint solver's predicted compatibility scores against observed benchmark results. For every evaluated stack, the engine computes a prediction residual: the difference between the predicted cumulative compatibility score and the normalized actual performance measured during benchmarking. These residuals are aggregated by constraint function, by component pair type, and by layer transition, revealing systematic biases in the constraint model. If the tokenizer compatibility function consistently overestimates compatibility for SentencePiece-to-BPE transitions by 0.12, the calibration engine adjusts the function's degradation coefficients downward and widens the confidence intervals for that transition type until prediction accuracy improves. If the orchestrator context budget function consistently underestimates throughput impact at low available token counts, the engine reshapes the throughput degradation curve to better match observed behavior. The calibration engine applies updates using an exponentially weighted moving average over recent evaluation cycles, with a configurable learning rate that balances responsiveness to new data against stability. Updates are bounded by configurable maximum adjustment limits per cycle to prevent a single anomalous benchmark result from destabilizing the constraint model. The calibration engine also tracks overall prediction accuracy as a meta-metric, monitoring whether the constraint model is improving over time. If prediction accuracy degrades, the engine flags the degradation for operator review and can optionally pause automatic updates.

This self-calibrating mechanism creates a compound advantage over systems that rely on statically defined constraints. As the system processes more evaluation cycles, its compatibility predictions become more precise, which improves its pruning accuracy, which reduces wasted evaluation resources, which allows more evaluation budget to be spent on genuinely promising candidates, which generates more calibration data. The result is a system that becomes more efficient and more accurate with use, a property that static dependency resolution cannot achieve because its constraints are authored by humans and only change when humans update them.

The result of probabilistic constraint propagation is a ranked compatibility graph where each valid connected subgraph carries a cumulative compatibility score and confidence interval. The Stack Assembler generates candidate stack manifests only from subgraphs whose cumulative scores exceed the organization's minimum threshold, ranked by predicted performance. Rather than evaluating every possible permutation, the assembler uses a guided search strategy informed by organizational policy hints (such as preferences for open-weight models, license exclusions, or cost ceilings), historical performance data from previous evaluation cycles, and the calibration engine's confidence assessments. Candidates with narrow confidence intervals and high predicted scores are prioritized because they represent the most reliable predictions. This further narrows the search space so that only the most promising valid combinations proceed to evaluation. Each candidate stack is expressed as an immutable manifest that pins every component version, configuration parameter, dependency, and predicted compatibility score, making it fully reproducible.

Candidate stacks that survive constraint propagation are submitted to an Evaluation Orchestrator that provisions isolated execution environments and runs them against the organization's benchmark suite. The benchmark suite is a versioned artifact containing representative tasks, golden answer datasets, latency budgets, and cost accounting rules. The orchestrator collects metrics across multiple objectives: task accuracy, end-to-end latency, token consumption, infrastructure cost, and any custom signals the organization defines such as compliance audit pass rates or fairness scores. All evaluation results are stored in an append-only Performance Ledger that preserves the complete history of every evaluation alongside the benchmark version used, ensuring that comparisons remain valid even as benchmarks evolve. Crucially, the ledger also stores the constraint solver's predicted compatibility scores for each evaluated candidate, enabling the calibration engine to compute prediction residuals.

A Policy Engine consumes the Performance Ledger and makes promotion decisions based on declarative rules authored by operators. Operators express criteria such as "promote a candidate only if it improves accuracy by at least two percent without increasing p99 latency beyond 300 milliseconds, and only if the constraint solver's confidence interval width for the candidate was below 0.15." The policy engine supports multi-objective Pareto analysis, surfacing trade-offs between competing metrics explicitly rather than collapsing them into a single score. When a candidate satisfies all promotion criteria, the Policy Engine initiates a staged rollout through a Deployment Controller that shifts traffic gradually, monitors live signals, and automatically rolls back if regression thresholds are breached. The deployment controller integrates with the organization's existing service mesh or gateway infrastructure so that the optimization loop operates within established operational boundaries.

Each promoted stack carries a Stack Compatibility Manifest embedded in its deployment metadata. This manifest is a machine-readable document listing every component version in the stack, the interface contract version for each component, the probabilistic constraint functions that were evaluated with their predicted scores and confidence intervals, the calibration engine's current accuracy metrics for each constraint function, and a cryptographic provenance signature linking back to the evaluation evidence and the discovery events that introduced each component. The manifest appears in deployment annotations (such as Kubernetes pod annotations or labels), in registry metadata attached to promoted stack bundles, and in responses from the system's compatibility negotiation API endpoint. This endpoint accepts a set of proposed component versions and returns a probabilistic compatibility assessment: a predicted cumulative score with confidence interval, any constraint violations or degradation warnings, and resolution suggestions with their predicted score improvements. External tools and registries can query this endpoint to make informed compatibility decisions. The presence of these manifests in deployment metadata and the compatibility negotiation API protocol constitute externally observable fingerprints of the system's operation, distinguishable from manual stack assembly by their structured format, probabilistic constraint records, calibration metadata, and provenance signatures.

Throughout the lifecycle, a Provenance Tracker records every decision in a cryptographically signed, append-only ledger: why a candidate was assembled, which constraint functions evaluated its compatibility and at what predicted scores, which benchmark version evaluated it, what calibration adjustments were applied afterward, what policy rule promoted it, and what deployment strategy was used. This provenance chain gives operators a complete audit trail from any production stack configuration back to the raw discovery event that introduced its components and the calibration history that informed the constraint model's predictions. Because every prior stack manifest and its evaluation data are preserved, the system can revert to any previously validated configuration within seconds rather than requiring a manual rebuild.

To make the value proposition concrete: consider an organization running 50 agents across 12 distinct stack configurations. When a new model version or framework update is released, engineers must manually assess compatibility with each existing configuration. Without formalized interface contracts, each assessment requires reading changelogs, checking API compatibility, testing tokenizer behavior, and running integration tests, a process that typically consumes several hours per configuration. With 12 configurations and weekly ecosystem releases, the organization faces over 100 hours per month of compatibility assessment work, and roughly one in three migration attempts fails due to cross-layer conflicts that surface only during integration testing. The probabilistic constraint propagation system reduces compatibility assessment to seconds per candidate and eliminates wasted evaluation cycles on combinations predicted to fall below performance thresholds, recovering those engineering hours while preventing production incidents from incompatible stack deployments. As the calibration engine refines its predictions over successive evaluation cycles, the system's pruning accuracy improves: early cycles might achieve 70% prediction accuracy, but after several months of operation the system typically reaches above 90%, meaning nearly all pruned combinations would have genuinely failed evaluation and nearly all passed combinations genuinely succeed.

# --- Probabilistic Constraint Function Definitions ---
# These functions compute continuous compatibility scores
# with confidence intervals, not Boolean pass/fail verdicts.

constraint_functions:
  - name: tokenizer-compatibility
    source_layer: model
    target_layer: prompt_template
    type: probabilistic
    function: |
      IF target.token_budget_distribution[source.tokenizer.type] IS NULL:
        # No empirical data for this tokenizer type
        score = 0.50  # uncertain default
        confidence_interval = 0.25  # wide interval reflects ignorance
      ELSE:
        expected_tokens = target.token_budget_distribution[source.tokenizer.type].mean
        token_variance = target.token_budget_distribution[source.tokenizer.type].std_dev
        context_utilization = expected_tokens / source.context_window_tokens
        # Score decreases as prompt consumes more context
        score = max(0, 1.0 - (context_utilization * 2.0))
        # Confidence narrows with more empirical measurements
        n_measurements = len(target.token_budget_distribution[source.tokenizer.type].measured_on)
        confidence_interval = token_variance / (expected_tokens * sqrt(n_measurements))
      RETURN {score, confidence_interval, confidence_level: 0.90}
    calibration:
      current_bias: -0.03  # solver slightly overestimates; applied as correction
      last_calibrated: "2026-07-10T08:00:00Z"
      prediction_accuracy_last_30_days: 0.87

  - name: context-budget-impact
    source_layers: [model, prompt_template]
    target_layer: orchestration
    type: probabilistic
    function: |
      expected_prompt_tokens = prompt_template.token_budget_distribution[model.tokenizer.type].mean
      remaining_context = model.context_window_tokens - expected_prompt_tokens
      IF remaining_context < target.min_available_context_tokens:
        score = 0.0  # hard constraint: below absolute minimum
        confidence_interval = 0.0
      ELSE:
        # Interpolate on the throughput degradation curve
        truncation_rate = interpolate(target.throughput_degradation_curve, remaining_context)
        accuracy_impact = interpolate_accuracy(target.throughput_degradation_curve, remaining_context)
        score = 1.0 - accuracy_impact
        # Confidence depends on prompt token variance and curve granularity
        token_std = prompt_template.token_budget_distribution[model.tokenizer.type].std_dev
        context_range = [remaining_context - token_std, remaining_context + token_std]
        score_range = [
          1.0 - interpolate_accuracy(target.throughput_degradation_curve, context_range[0]),
          1.0 - interpolate_accuracy(target.throughput_degradation_curve, context_range[1])
        ]
        confidence_interval = abs(score_range[1] - score_range[0]) / 2
      RETURN {score, confidence_interval, confidence_level: 0.90}
    calibration:
      current_bias: +0.05  # solver underestimates; orchestrator handles truncation better than predicted
      last_calibrated: "2026-07-12T12:00:00Z"
      prediction_accuracy_last_30_days: 0.82

  - name: model-capabilities-match
    source_layer: model
    target_layer: prompt_template
    type: hard  # this remains Boolean; capabilities either exist or do not
    expression: |
      target.required_model_capabilities IS SUBSET OF source.capabilities
    failure_message: >
      Template requires capabilities not supported by model

  - name: runtime-resource-satisfaction
    source_layer: model
    target_layer: runtime
    type: hard  # resource requirements are binary
    expression: |
      source.resource_requirements.gpu_memory_gb <= target.gpu_memory_gb
      AND source.resource_requirements.required_features
        IS SUBSET OF target.available_features
    failure_message: >
      Model requires {source.resource_requirements.gpu_memory_gb}GB GPU
      but runtime provides {target.gpu_memory_gb}GB

**Cross-Layer Probabilistic Compatibility Propagation with Self-Calibrating Constraints for Autonomous AI Agent Stack Assembly**

# Problem Statement

AI agent deployments are built from multiple interdependent software layers: foundation models, prompt templates, orchestration frameworks, tool connectors, and runtime environments. Upgrading any single layer can break the others through cross-layer interactions that nobody has formally quantified. This is not like traditional package dependencies where version mismatches produce hard failures. AI stack incompatibilities show up as continuous performance degradation. A tokenizer change will not crash a prompt template, but it will silently inflate its token consumption, and accuracy drops by a measurable amount that only surfaces after expensive benchmark runs. Engineers discover these probabilistic incompatibilities through trial and error.

With weekly ecosystem releases and organizations running dozens of agents, the compatibility assessment burden compounds fast. No existing system models cross-layer compatibility as a probabilistic constraint problem. None reason about continuous degradation gradients across all stack layers at once. And none refine their own compatibility predictions from observed outcomes.

# Description of Invention

## Novel Step

We introduce a probabilistic cross-layer compatibility propagation mechanism that models every AI agent stack component as a node in a compatibility graph. Edges encode machine-readable interface contracts that express compatibility as continuous confidence scores rather than Boolean pass/fail verdicts. When a new component is discovered from external registries, the system performs probabilistic constraint propagation across this graph, computing expected compatibility scores and confidence intervals for each candidate stack combination. The propagation reasons about transitive degradation gradients: a model's tokenizer vocabulary change may inflate a prompt template's effective token consumption by an estimated 35% to 45%, which narrows the context budget available for tool call results in the orchestration layer, which we predict reduces end-to-end task accuracy by 8% to 12% with 90% confidence. Combinations whose predicted compatibility falls below configurable thresholds get pruned before any evaluation infrastructure is provisioned.

Critically, we include a closed-loop calibration mechanism. After each evaluation cycle, observed benchmark results are compared against the constraint solver's predictions, and the system automatically adjusts predicate thresholds, confidence interval widths, and degradation coefficients to improve future prediction accuracy. This self-calibrating constraint model has no analog in traditional dependency resolution systems (apt, npm, Helm, Kubernetes OLM), which resolve hard version constraints and cannot express or learn from continuous compatibility gradients. Each promoted stack carries a standardized Stack Compatibility Manifest embedded in deployment metadata and queryable through a compatibility negotiation API, producing externally detectable artifacts that distinguish this system from ad hoc integration approaches.

## How It Works

We model the AI agent software stack as a directed compatibility graph. Each node represents a versioned component: a specific model release, a prompt template revision, an orchestration framework version, a tool connector build, or a runtime configuration. Edges between nodes carry probabilistic interface contracts, which are machine-readable declarations of what each component provides to and requires from adjacent layers. These are expressed as continuous compatibility functions rather than Boolean predicates.

Every component in the system carries an interface contract expressed in a standardized metadata schema with both hard constraints and soft compatibility parameters. For a foundation model, the contract declares the tokenizer type, vocabulary size, maximum context window in tokens, supported input and output formats (chat completion, raw completion, function calling), resource requirements (GPU memory, system memory, compute features such as specific CUDA versions or attention implementations), and explicit incompatibilities as hard constraints. It also declares soft parameters: measured token density ratios for common text types (English prose, code, structured JSON), empirical latency profiles under different quantization levels, and historical accuracy baselines on reference tasks.

For a prompt template, the contract declares hard constraints such as required model capabilities (tool calling support, system prompt handling) and input/output variable schemas. Soft parameters include the token budget expressed as a distribution across tokenizer families. A template might consume 1800 to 2200 tokens with SentencePiece tokenizers and 1600 to 1900 with BPE, depending on content. It also includes sensitivity coefficients that quantify how much accuracy degrades per percentage of context budget consumed, and a compatibility history recording observed performance with specific model versions. For an orchestration framework, the contract declares supported chain patterns, maximum tool call depth, memory backend requirements, and minimum available context token thresholds as hard constraints. Soft parameters capture throughput degradation curves as context use approaches limits. For a runtime environment, the contract declares available compute features, memory limits, supported container images, and scaling characteristics, with soft parameters expressing performance variability under different load levels.

The Component Discovery Service periodically polls external registries, including model hubs, package repositories, and internal artifact stores, and normalizes each discovered component into this contract schema. Staleness detection runs on a configurable cadence so that deprecated or withdrawn components are flagged and excluded from future candidate generation. When a new component is ingested, the system inserts the corresponding node into the compatibility graph and evaluates probabilistic constraint functions on every edge connecting the new node to existing nodes in adjacent layers.

A constraint function differs fundamentally from the Boolean predicates used in traditional dependency resolution. Rather than returning true or false, each constraint function returns a compatibility score between 0.0 and 1.0 along with a confidence interval reflecting the system's certainty in that estimate. For example, a tokenizer compatibility function between a model and a prompt template does not merely check whether tokenizer types match. Instead, it computes the expected token count variance when the template is tokenized by the model's tokenizer, derives a predicted accuracy impact from the template's sensitivity coefficients, and produces a compatibility score such as 0.72 with a confidence interval of plus or minus 0.08 at 90% confidence. That 0.72 means the combination is expected to retain 72% of baseline accuracy for that cross-layer interaction. It is not a probability of success. This continuous representation captures the reality that AI stack incompatibilities are not binary: a tokenizer mismatch does not crash the system but degrades performance by a quantifiable amount that may or may not be acceptable depending on organizational policy.

When a new component is added to the graph, the system performs forward probabilistic constraint propagation through all downstream layers. The algorithm works in three stages. First, it evaluates all direct constraint functions between the new component and every existing component in the adjacent layer, computing pairwise compatibility scores with confidence intervals. Second, for each pairing that exceeds the minimum score threshold, it propagates forward to the next layer: given a particular model paired with a particular prompt template, their combined characteristics (effective available context after prompt consumption, accumulated resource footprint, predicted accuracy retention) feed into constraint functions against each candidate orchestration framework. Compatibility scores compose multiplicatively across layers, so a 0.85 model-to-prompt score combined with a 0.90 prompt-to-orchestrator score yields a cumulative cross-layer score of approximately 0.77. Third, propagation continues through tool connectors and runtime layers, accumulating both resource requirements and compounding compatibility scores. The confidence intervals widen as propagation deepens, reflecting increasing uncertainty in multi-hop predictions.

This probabilistic propagation is where the system's value becomes concrete and where it diverges most sharply from traditional dependency resolution. Consider a tokenizer vocabulary expansion in a new model release. A traditional Boolean constraint system would either pass or fail based on a type match check. Our system instead computes that the vocabulary expansion will increase the prompt template's token consumption by an estimated 38% (confidence interval: 33% to 43%), which reduces the effective context available for the orchestration layer's tool call results from 12,000 tokens to approximately 7,400 tokens. The orchestration layer's throughput degradation curve indicates that at 7,400 available tokens, tool call truncation will occur in roughly 15% of invocations. Composing these effects, we predict a cumulative accuracy retention of 0.71 with a confidence interval of 0.65 to 0.77 for the full stack. If organizational policy requires a minimum cumulative score of 0.80, this combination is pruned without provisioning any infrastructure, but it is preserved as a near-miss candidate that could become viable if the prompt template is revised to reduce its token footprint. A Boolean solver cannot express this kind of graduated analysis. It cannot distinguish between a combination that misses the threshold by 0.01 and one that scores 0.15.

The self-calibrating feedback loop is the mechanism that makes the constraint model improve over time, and it has no counterpart in traditional dependency resolution systems. After each evaluation cycle, the Calibration Engine compares the constraint solver's predicted compatibility scores against observed benchmark results. For every evaluated stack, the engine computes a prediction residual: the difference between the predicted cumulative compatibility score and the normalized actual performance measured during benchmarking. These residuals are aggregated by constraint function, by component pair type, and by layer transition, revealing systematic biases in the constraint model.

If the tokenizer compatibility function consistently overestimates compatibility for SentencePiece-to-BPE transitions by 0.12, the calibration engine adjusts the function's degradation coefficients downward and widens the confidence intervals for that transition type until prediction accuracy improves. If the orchestrator context budget function consistently underestimates throughput impact at low available token counts, the engine reshapes the throughput degradation curve to better match observed behavior. Updates are applied using an exponentially weighted moving average over recent evaluation cycles, with a configurable learning rate that balances responsiveness to new data against stability. Updates are bounded by configurable maximum adjustment limits per cycle to prevent a single anomalous benchmark result from destabilizing the constraint model. The calibration engine also tracks overall prediction accuracy as a meta-metric. If prediction accuracy degrades, the engine flags the degradation for operator review and can optionally pause automatic updates.

What this self-calibrating mechanism creates is a compound advantage over systems that rely on statically defined constraints. As the system processes more evaluation cycles, its compatibility predictions become more precise, which improves pruning accuracy, which reduces wasted evaluation resources, which lets more evaluation budget go toward genuinely promising candidates, which generates more calibration data. The result is a system that becomes more efficient and more accurate with use. Static dependency resolution cannot achieve this property because its constraints are authored by humans and only change when humans update them.

The result of probabilistic constraint propagation is a ranked compatibility graph where each valid connected subgraph carries a cumulative compatibility score and confidence interval. The Stack Assembler generates candidate stack manifests only from subgraphs whose cumulative scores exceed the organization's minimum threshold, ranked by predicted performance. Rather than evaluating every possible permutation, the assembler uses a guided search strategy informed by organizational policy hints (such as preferences for open-weight models, license exclusions, or cost ceilings), historical performance data from previous evaluation cycles, and the calibration engine's confidence assessments. Candidates with narrow confidence intervals and high predicted scores are prioritized because they represent the most reliable predictions. This further narrows the search space so that only the most promising valid combinations proceed to evaluation. Each candidate stack is expressed as an immutable manifest that pins every component version, configuration parameter, dependency, and predicted compatibility score, making it fully reproducible.

Candidate stacks that survive constraint propagation are submitted to an Evaluation Orchestrator that provisions isolated execution environments and runs them against the organization's benchmark suite. The benchmark suite is a versioned artifact containing representative tasks, golden answer datasets, latency budgets, and cost accounting rules. The orchestrator collects metrics across multiple objectives: task accuracy, end-to-end latency, token consumption, infrastructure cost, and any custom signals the organization defines such as compliance audit pass rates or fairness scores. All evaluation results are stored in an append-only Performance Ledger that preserves the complete history of every evaluation alongside the benchmark version used, making sure that comparisons remain valid even as benchmarks evolve. The ledger also stores the constraint solver's predicted compatibility scores for each evaluated candidate, enabling the calibration engine to compute prediction residuals.

A Policy Engine consumes the Performance Ledger and makes promotion decisions based on declarative rules authored by operators. Operators express criteria such as "promote a candidate only if it improves accuracy by at least two percent without increasing p99 latency beyond 300 milliseconds, and only if the constraint solver's confidence interval width for the candidate was below 0.15." The policy engine supports multi-objective Pareto analysis, surfacing trade-offs between competing metrics explicitly rather than collapsing them into a single score. When a candidate satisfies all promotion criteria, the Policy Engine initiates a staged rollout through a Deployment Controller that shifts traffic gradually, monitors live signals, and automatically rolls back if regression thresholds are breached. The deployment controller integrates with the organization's existing service mesh or gateway infrastructure so that the optimization loop operates within established operational boundaries.

Each promoted stack carries a Stack Compatibility Manifest embedded in its deployment metadata. This manifest is a machine-readable document listing every component version in the stack, the interface contract version for each component, the probabilistic constraint functions that were evaluated with their predicted scores and confidence intervals, the calibration engine's current accuracy metrics for each constraint function, and a cryptographic provenance signature linking back to the evaluation evidence and the discovery events that introduced each component. The manifest appears in deployment annotations (such as Kubernetes pod annotations or labels), in registry metadata attached to promoted stack bundles, and in responses from the system's compatibility negotiation API endpoint. This endpoint accepts a set of proposed component versions and returns a probabilistic compatibility assessment: a predicted cumulative score with confidence interval, any constraint violations or degradation warnings, and resolution suggestions with their predicted score improvements. External tools and registries can query this endpoint to make informed compatibility decisions. The presence of these manifests in deployment metadata and the compatibility negotiation API protocol constitute externally observable fingerprints of the system's operation, distinguishable from manual stack assembly by their structured format, probabilistic constraint records, calibration metadata, and provenance signatures.

Throughout the lifecycle, a Provenance Tracker records every decision in a cryptographically signed, append-only ledger: why a candidate was assembled, which constraint functions evaluated its compatibility and at what predicted scores, which benchmark version evaluated it, what calibration adjustments were applied afterward, what policy rule promoted it, and what deployment strategy was used. This provenance chain gives operators a full audit trail from any production stack configuration back to the raw discovery event that introduced its components and the calibration history that informed the constraint model's predictions. Because every prior stack manifest and its evaluation data are preserved, the system can revert to any previously validated configuration within seconds rather than requiring a manual rebuild.

To make the value proposition concrete: consider an organization running 50 agents across 12 distinct stack configurations. When a new model version or framework update ships, engineers have to manually assess compatibility with each existing configuration. Without formalized interface contracts, each assessment requires reading changelogs, checking API compatibility, testing tokenizer behavior, and running integration tests. That process typically eats several hours per configuration. With 12 configurations and weekly ecosystem releases, the organization faces over 100 hours per month of compatibility assessment work, and roughly one in three migration attempts fails due to cross-layer conflicts that surface only during integration testing. Our probabilistic constraint propagation system reduces compatibility assessment to seconds per candidate and eliminates wasted evaluation cycles on combinations predicted to fall below performance thresholds. This recovers those engineering hours while preventing production incidents from incompatible stack deployments. As the calibration engine refines its predictions over successive evaluation cycles, pruning accuracy improves: early cycles might achieve 70% prediction accuracy, but after several months of operation the system typically reaches above 90%. That means nearly all pruned combinations would have genuinely failed evaluation and nearly all passed combinations genuinely succeed.

# --- Probabilistic Constraint Function Definitions ---
# These functions compute continuous compatibility scores
# with confidence intervals, not Boolean pass/fail verdicts.

constraint_functions:
  - name: tokenizer-compatibility
    source_layer: model
    target_layer: prompt_template
    type: probabilistic
    function: |
      IF target.token_budget_distribution[source.tokenizer.type] IS NULL:
        # No empirical data for this tokenizer type
        score = 0.50  # uncertain default
        confidence_interval = 0.25  # wide interval reflects ignorance
      ELSE:
        expected_tokens = target.token_budget_distribution[source.tokenizer.type].mean
        token_variance = target.token_budget_distribution[source.tokenizer.type].std_dev
        context_utilization = expected_tokens / source.context_window_tokens
        # Score decreases as prompt consumes more context
        score = max(0, 1.0 - (context_utilization * 2.0))
        # Confidence narrows with more empirical measurements
        n_measurements = len(target.token_budget_distribution[source.tokenizer.type].measured_on)
        confidence_interval = token_variance / (expected_tokens * sqrt(n_measurements))
      RETURN {score, confidence_interval, confidence_level: 0.90}
    calibration:
      current_bias: -0.03  # solver slightly overestimates; applied as correction
      last_calibrated: "2026-07-10T08:00:00Z"
      prediction_accuracy_last_30_days: 0.87

  - name: context-budget-impact
    source_layers: [model, prompt_template]
    target_layer: orchestration
    type: probabilistic
    function: |
      expected_prompt_tokens = prompt_template.token_budget_distribution[model.tokenizer.type].mean
      remaining_context = model.context_window_tokens - expected_prompt_tokens
      IF remaining_context < target.min_available_context_tokens:
        score = 0.0  # hard constraint: below absolute minimum
        confidence_interval = 0.0
      ELSE:
        # Interpolate on the throughput degradation curve
        truncation_rate = interpolate(target.throughput_degradation_curve, remaining_context)
        accuracy_impact = interpolate_accuracy(target.throughput_degradation_curve, remaining_context)
        score = 1.0 - accuracy_impact
        # Confidence depends on prompt token variance and curve granularity
        token_std = prompt_template.token_budget_distribution[model.tokenizer.type].std_dev
        context_range = [remaining_context - token_std, remaining_context + token_std]
        score_range = [
          1.0 - interpolate_accuracy(target.throughput_degradation_curve, context_range[0]),
          1.0 - interpolate_accuracy(target.throughput_degradation_curve, context_range[1])
        ]
        confidence_interval = abs(score_range[1] - score_range[0]) / 2
      RETURN {score, confidence_interval, confidence_level: 0.90}
    calibration:
      current_bias: +0.05  # solver underestimates; orchestrator handles truncation better than predicted
      last_calibrated: "2026-07-12T12:00:00Z"
      prediction_accuracy_last_30_days: 0.82

  - name: model-capabilities-match
    source_layer: model
    target_layer: prompt_template
    type: hard  # this remains Boolean; capabilities either exist or do not
    expression: |
      target.required_model_capabilities IS SUBSET OF source.capabilities
    failure_message: >
      Template requires capabilities not supported by model

  - name: runtime-resource-satisfaction
    source_layer: model
    target_layer: runtime
    type: hard  # resource requirements are binary
    expression: |
      source.resource_requirements.gpu_memory_gb <= target.gpu_memory_gb
      AND source.resource_requirements.required_features
        IS SUBSET OF target.available_features
    failure_message: >
      Model requires {source.resource_requirements.gpu_memory_gb}GB GPU
      but runtime provides {target.gpu_memory_gb}GB

# Prior Art

**TL;DR**: Existing systems optimize individual layers of ML pipelines (AutoML, NAS, prompt tuning), manage infrastructure deployment (Terraform, ArgoCD), track experiments (MLflow, W&B), or resolve Boolean package dependencies (apt, npm, Helm, OLM). None of them model cross-layer AI stack compatibility as a probabilistic constraint problem with continuous degradation scores. None include a self-calibrating feedback loop that refines constraint predictions from observed evaluation outcomes. The combination of probabilistic constraint propagation across all agent stack layers, self-calibrating constraint functions, and detectable compatibility manifests is not present in any prior system, as far as we can tell.

**Advantages**: This invention introduces two specific mechanisms that we believe no prior system provides. First, a probabilistic compatibility graph where constraint functions return continuous scores with confidence intervals, capturing the reality that AI stack incompatibilities produce graduated performance degradation rather than binary failures. This is fundamentally different from the Boolean satisfiability model used by package managers and operator lifecycle managers. Second, a self-calibrating feedback loop where observed benchmark results automatically refine constraint function parameters, making the system's predictions more accurate over time without human intervention. Traditional dependency resolution systems have no learning capability; their constraints are statically authored and only change when humans update them. The Stack Compatibility Manifest (with probabilistic scores and calibration metadata) and Compatibility Negotiation API create externally observable artifacts that distinguish the system from both manual integration approaches and Boolean dependency solvers.

## Key Differentiators

1. **Probabilistic Cross-Layer Constraint Propagation**: Unlike package managers (apt, npm, Helm), operator lifecycle managers (OLM), and single-layer optimizers (AutoML, NAS, prompt tuning), we model cross-layer compatibility as continuous scores with confidence intervals rather than Boolean satisfiability. Our constraint functions capture the reality that AI stack incompatibilities produce graduated performance degradation, not binary failures. A tokenizer mismatch does not crash the system; it inflates token consumption by a quantifiable amount that compounds through downstream layers. This continuous representation enables graduated pruning: combinations that narrowly miss thresholds are preserved as near-miss candidates, while clearly incompatible combinations are eliminated. A Boolean solver simply cannot make that distinction.

2. **Self-Calibrating Constraint Model**: The closed-loop calibration mechanism, where observed benchmark results automatically refine constraint function parameters (bias corrections, confidence interval widths, degradation coefficients), is genuinely new as far as we know. Traditional dependency resolution systems (apt, OLM, Helm) use statically authored constraints that only change when humans update package metadata. AutoML surrogate models learn performance surfaces but not cross-layer compatibility gradients. Our constraint model improves its own prediction accuracy over time without human intervention, creating a compound efficiency advantage: better predictions produce better pruning, which focuses evaluation budget on stronger candidates, which generates more informative calibration data. We have not found any prior system in dependency resolution, MLOps, or AutoML literature that combines cross-layer compatibility prediction with automated self-calibration.

3. **Detectable Artifacts with Probabilistic Metadata**: Each promoted stack carries a machine-readable manifest in deployment metadata that records probabilistic constraint scores, confidence intervals, calibration metadata (prediction accuracy, bias corrections), and cryptographic provenance signatures. The compatibility negotiation API endpoint returns probabilistic verdicts with constraint model accuracy metadata. These artifacts create externally observable fingerprints that distinguish the system from both manual integration approaches and Boolean dependency solvers, which matters for the enforceability requirement for patent protection. The presence of continuous scores, confidence intervals, and calibration metadata in deployment annotations and API responses is detectable through standard observability tooling and cannot be replicated by traditional Boolean constraint solvers.
